metadata.file_name: A meta-analysis on the relationship between school characteristics and student outcomes in science and maths   evidence from large-scale studies.pdf
metadata.title: A meta-analysis on the relationship between school characteristics and student outcomes in science and maths: evidence from large-scale studies

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This meta-analysis synthesizes effect sizes transformed to correlation coefficients from 71 empirical quantitative studies based on large-scale national and international assessments (e.g., PISA, TIMSS, NAEP and other longitudinal U.S. studies). Because the unit of analysis is the extracted effect size (and the authors conduct multilevel meta-analyses with clustering at the sample level), the paper does not report the application of student-level sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures from any single ILSA dataset. Instead, the weighting logic is internal to the meta-analytic model (random-effects and multilevel metaSEM), not survey-weighted estimation of achievement scores. For replication with ILSA microdata, analysts would need to apply the original assessment’s complex survey weights (and PV procedures for cognitive achievement outcomes) within each primary study before computing comparable effect sizes.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a meta-analysis of previously published large-scale studies where the authors extract and transform reported effects into correlation coefficients; it does not perform student-level modeling on ILSA plausible values (PVs). PV handling is therefore not applicable to the meta-analytic dataset constructed from effect sizes rather than raw assessment microdata. Missing-data handling for PVs or item nonresponse is also not reported because the analysis is based on extracted effect sizes from primary studies, not on re-estimation from incomplete microdata.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The meta-analysis included 71 empirical quantitative studies from large-scale projects (secondary education level) published in English and peer-reviewed, with sufficient reported statistics to compute or transform effect sizes. The authors searched ERIC and Web of Science (2000–2016) using keyword combinations for school variables, cognitive and motivational-aﬀective student outcomes, and science/maths, then applied inclusion criteria requiring thematic fit, subject relevance (science or maths), secondary-level samples, and availability of parameters for effect-size transformation. They excluded studies that were elementary/primary-only (including cases where only grade six or below was sampled), and when studies included both elementary and secondary schools they retained only secondary-school effect sizes when reported separately. They also excluded effect sizes when standardization was impossible due to missing standard deviations (or invalid values), and they removed identified outlier effect sizes (beyond ±3 SD) for sensitivity checks but retained the full set after re-analysis showed no meaningful change.

The authors extracted relationships between school characteristics (e.g., academic press, school climate, material and personnel resources, classroom climate, instructional practices, and out-of-school activities) and student outcomes in science and maths, distinguishing cognitive versus motivational-aﬀective outcomes and science versus maths. They transformed diverse primary-study effect metrics into correlation coefficients and estimated multilevel random-effects meta-analytic models using metaSEM, clustering at the sample level to address dependency among effect sizes. Overall, the mean effect was r = .15 (95% CI [.12, .17], p < .01), with heterogeneity (I2 = .89 within-sample). The strongest positive associations were for SES composition (r = .30), followed by out-of-school activities (r = .18), academic press (r = .14), instructional practices (r = .13), and classroom climate (r = .13), while material and personnel resources were near zero. The authors emphasize that effects are correlational and cannot support causal claims. data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is a systematic meta-analysis/review of previously published large-scale studies rather than an empirical study that trains predictive models on ILSA microdata. Consequently, there is no single ILSA program/cycle/grade/domain dataset used for student-level ML, no PV handling or missing-data imputation performed on raw assessment responses, and no ML algorithm comparison. The extracted quantitative results are meta-analytic effect sizes (correlations) rather than model performance metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE) from an ML pipeline.
